processing: Darjeeling black tea made by the orthodox method; first flush lots of this kind are only lightly oxidised for a black tea. Some lots are sold as organic in the FTGFOP1 grade.
harvest_season: First flush is the lot most often seen under this name. In Darjeeling generally it falls from about late February to mid-April.
appearance_dry: As with other Darjeeling first flushes, a mix of olive-green and brown leaf with pale tips.
appearance_liquor: A pale golden amber, typical of Darjeeling first flush.
appearance_wet: Typically greenish leaf with some coppery edges, as with other first flushes.
taste_profile: Few tasting notes exist for this garden; as with other Darjeeling first flushes, expect a light, floral, slightly astringent cup.

brewing.notes: General first flush guidance: water a little off the boil and no milk. Long steeps make these teas sharp.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush, as Darjeeling normally is, with the garden name and grade on the label: one organic lot is sold as FTGFOP1 first flush. First flush is best within a year or so of picking.
description:
Soureni, also written Sourenee, is a Darjeeling garden around Soureni Bazar, about 7 km from Mirik on the alternate road between Darjeeling and Siliguri. Mechi and several other estates are its neighbours.

What reaches shops abroad is mostly organic first flush in the FTGFOP1 grade. As is typical of the season, that means a lightly oxidised black tea that looks and drinks closer to oolong than to Assam.

Detailed notes on this garden are scarce, so don't count on the muscatel flavour some sellers attach to the name of the region. Darjeeling first flush usually tastes floral and fresh, with a little bite. Use cooler water than you would for a stronger black tea and leave out the milk.

Check the year and flush on the label. A first flush that is a few years old will have lost most of what you are paying for.
history:
The land belonged to Dakman Rai, a Nepali sardar who received large tracts from the British as Darjeeling's tea gardens were being set up. His son Bhoujit Rai planted some tea here, then sold the estate to the brothers Ramlal and Jalooram Tiwari, who had come from Rajasthan to Darjeeling in 1870 and kept a shop in Kurseong.

The Tiwaris formally established the Soureni Tea Estate in 1902 and sold it in 1990. Titagarh Wagons has since been named as the owner, though that may have changed.
